name: crystalline NH3 ice (its absorption not drawn)
paper: J. V. Martonchik, G. S. Orton and J. F. Appleby, "Optical properties of NH3 ice from the far infrared to the near ultraviolet", Appl. Opt. 23 (1984) 541–547, DOI 10.1364/AO.23.000541, for n, and for the k rows between its 1,462 and 200 nm rows, which this file shows to be interpolations and does not draw
source: optool, lnk_data/nh3-m-Martonchik1983.lnk, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cdominik/optool/0b1fa6df95e3a694dc64abdbf8e36dad127165ab/lnk_data/nh3-m-Martonchik1983.lnk, SHA-256 14a5b66bb35101a89cacb07cd80585413ee4aa8986d966138d866ffd4fb9babd, fetched 2026-10-09. R08.T5.i's search for a measured visible absorption of NH3 ice (2026-10-16) found none, nor a measured bound on it, for the solid. The liquid's measured total attenuation (C. W. Robertson and D. Williams, "Lambert absorption coefficient of liquid ammonia in the visible region", J. Opt. Soc. Am. 63 (1973) 763, DOI 10.1364/JOSA.63.000763, Table I, read on the journal's page, https://opg.optica.org/josa/abstract.cfm?uri=josa-63-6-763, SHA-256 802a0b942b36a10c61509c62e6977e803a8b4fa37a04d61f7ed01b4d0c14beeb, fetched 2026-10-16, as ammonia-liquid.json cites it) bounds the liquid's k by 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ at 400 nm and 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ at 654 nm (k = αλ ÷ 4π, computed), 17 and 136 times below the fill's k there, on a sample whose temperature and purity the page does not state. Hapke, Wells, Wagner and Partlow 1981 (Icarus 47, 361, DOI 10.1016/0019-1035(81)90184-6; closed; its abstract at NASA NTRS 19820033673, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19820033673, SHA-256 7249b50d768713b24b5a8a691817669776ffe1407c430cd8559b1cf72b493281) measure frosts' reflectance over 0.1–2.5 µm, "NH3 is bright at wavelengths longer than 0.21 microns, where reflectance drops to a value of only a few per cent at shorter wavelengths"; Wagner, Hapke and Wells 1987 (Icarus 69, 14, DOI 10.1016/0019-1035(87)90003-0; closed; its abstract at NTRS 19870044303, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19870044303, SHA-256 3c7ec35217257030126c23f11bb9b8530880a1d5212b9984bda17bfee1e8a9d6) give an atlas of reflectance over 92–1800 nm with NH3 frost among the frosts. Neither gives k: they are the visible frost reflectances for P14.T49.i to invert. Pipes, Browell and Anderson 1974 (Icarus 21, 283, DOI 10.1016/0019-1035(74)90043-8; closed; its title through Crossref, https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0019-1035(74)90043-8, SHA-256 ee41413eb0b6cc82274e6acb0de1752cdea2562652577831e64328f6c7a5e10f) reach 1400–3000 Å only. Browell and Anderson 1975 (J. Opt. Soc. Am. 65, 919, DOI 10.1364/JOSA.65.000919; closed; its abstract through OpenAlex, https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1364/JOSA.65.000919, SHA-256 ab7cf61eac917a62e0f3b70adc8ed6df7138cb2079059608011041fd0f85ce57) give n of amorphous NH3 ice over 1925–3200 Å, and upper limits on its absorption at 1760 Å only. Hudson, Gerakines and Yarnall 2022 (Astrophys. J. 925, 156, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ac3e74; its abstract through OpenAlex, https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.3847/1538-4357/ac3e74, SHA-256 e6acf9d02b881e941edba56f6a3e37c633a24b6e4497559b19aec0844fa36927) give infrared optical constants and n at 670 nm. Howett, Carlson, Irwin and Calcutt 2007 (J. Opt. Soc. Am. B 24, 126, DOI 10.1364/JOSAB.24.000126; closed; the journal's abstract page, https://opg.optica.org/josab/abstract.cfm?uri=josab-24-1-126, SHA-256 f3f952d8c413c5fdafa928451f294dc3808e7bd53bc5ad91694f0fc94ec4f630) measure thin-film transmission over 1300–12,000 cm⁻¹ (0.83–7.7 µm), and their Table 1 of earlier work on NH3 ice lists none in the visible but Martonchik et al.'s. Kieffer 1974 ("Ring particle sizes and composition derived from eclipse cooling curves and reflection spectra", in The Rings of Saturn, NASA, 1974; NTRS 19750009169, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19750009169/downloads/19750009169.pdf, SHA-256 d542cec141d79e43819a3b5d497c1f60b0f617d44d58876ff4593a04905da7b3, read in full) shows NH3 frost spectra over about 1.25–3 µm only (its Fig. 1). Lebofsky and Fegley 1976 ("Laboratory reflection spectra for the determination of chemical composition of icy bodies", Icarus 28, 379, DOI 10.1016/0019-1035(76)90151-2; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/0019-1035(76)90151-2, SHA-256 ddb3457e0de897d377a75d28496c42d30b6ac32a14d0a709914267986f7f2708) and Rosen and Pipkin 1978 ("Reflectance spectra for sodium and potassium doped ammonia frosts: Implications for Io's surface", Icarus 35, 252, DOI 10.1016/0019-1035(78)90010-6; https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1016/0019-1035(78)90010-6, SHA-256 16f405f46b5503c8001b22fdc371c0e467d31e900a17ba76ba6e1fe9c3fb37fc) are closed, their titles alone reachable

reduction: n linear in wavelength between the source's rows, onto 380–780 nm every 5 nm, to six significant figures; the source has rows at 320, 433, 668 and 1,462 nm here, so n is interpolated between them; the copy states no temperature. k = 0 at every grid point, a stated stand-in (R08.T5.i, decision-p14-t49c-split §5.3), since the paper's k rows between its 1,462 and 200 nm rows are interpolations, not measurements, and no measured visible absorption was found (the file's source). Its Table I (the journal's abstract page, https://opg.optica.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-23-4-541, SHA-256 42ed721929a8baeeae4a1ed0f79970bf0c6fc46e93b56c0e46156a3e4bc83092, fetched 2026-10-16) has two rows between 1,462 and 320 nm, 14,976.7 cm⁻¹ (668 nm, k 3.963 × 10⁻⁵) and 23,113.3 cm⁻¹ (433 nm, 2.109 × 10⁻⁵), at one and two thirds of the interval between its 6,840 cm⁻¹ row (k 5.817 × 10⁻⁵) and its 31,250 cm⁻¹ row (2.546 × 10⁻⁶); they equal the linear interpolation in k between those rows to four figures, 3.9629 × 10⁻⁵ and 2.1087 × 10⁻⁵, where a fill linear in log k would give 2.05 × 10⁻⁵ and 7.22 × 10⁻⁶ (computed). Every row from 200 to 320 nm lies on k = 1.592 × 10⁻⁶ + 7.95 × 10⁻⁹ (λ − 200 nm) within a unit of the table's last figure (computed). So 380–780 nm lies wholly on interpolations: 380–433 nm runs towards the 320 nm row, an end of the 200–320 nm line, and 668–780 nm towards the 1,462 nm row, at the edge of the 1.5 µm band (Table I's k reaches 2.693 × 10⁻⁴ at 6,500 cm⁻¹). The paper's abstract says only that the real index was "obtained from previously published spectra of the absorption index ni by means of the Kramers-Kronig dispersion relation", and does not name the visible's source (OpenAlex's record, https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1364/AO.23.000541, SHA-256 6dd81d6a76cdc19ad45c89c21d9d3226fa3eb4d3121a7c4e5fec05203e97b4e0, fetched 2026-10-16). As R08.T5.b reduced it, k was 2.88714 × 10⁻⁵ at 550 nm, an absorption length of 1.5 mm (computed), which makes a white frost come out at a normal albedo of 0.29 in P14.T49.c's model (decision-p14-t49c-split ruling 5). k = 0 draws the colourless crystal lossless, an upper bound on its brightness, as the k = 0 ices are (decision-p14-t49c-split §5.6), and Hapke et al. 1981's bright frost agrees with it (the file's source); the crystal's weak N–H overtone bands are not drawn. n is not part of the fill: the rows' 1.423 and 1.449 at 668 and 433 nm lie off the straight line between the 1,462 and 320 nm rows' n (1.4347 and 1.4613, computed), and n stays as reduced
standIn: a crystal whose visible absorption is not drawn: Martonchik et al.'s visible k is a fill between their 1462 nm and 320 nm values, not a measurement, and no measured visible absorption of NH3 ice was found, so k = 0, an upper bound on its brightness; its real index is theirs
